title: TOEFL iBT Reading Practice Test 27
instructions: Read each passage carefully and answer all questions. You have 35 minutes. Questions test factual understanding, vocabulary, inference, and the ability to identify main ideas.

passages.title: The History of Cartography
passages.text:
Cartography — the science and art of map-making — has evolved dramatically across human history, serving as both a practical tool for navigation and a reflection of how societies understand their world. From ancient clay tablets depicting Mesopotamian territories to modern digital satellite maps, cartography reveals not only where places are, but also what knowledge societies valued, how they organised space, and what they believed about distant regions. The history of cartography thus illuminates broader questions about human geography, exploration, cultural knowledge, and technological capability.

Early maps were created for specific practical purposes: temple or palace administrators needed to track land holdings, armies needed to plan campaigns, and merchants required information about trade routes. The ancient Babylonians created maps on clay tablets around 2300 BCE, primarily representing property and natural features relevant to agricultural irrigation. Ancient Egyptian maps from around 1400 BCE depicted minerals, quarries, and settlements essential to their economy. These early maps were relatively crude by modern standards, but they served their intended audiences and demonstrated sophisticated spatial reasoning. Greek scholars, particularly Eratosthenes and Strabo, made foundational contributions: Eratosthenes calculated Earth's circumference with remarkable accuracy around 240 BCE, and Strabo synthesised geographical knowledge from across the Mediterranean world.

The Islamic Golden Age, spanning from roughly the 8th to 14th centuries, was a period of extraordinary cartographic achievement. Arab geographers and mathematicians refined map projection techniques and created detailed maps of the known world. Al-Idrisi, a 12th-century Arab geographer, prepared the Tabula Rogeriana, one of the most accurate and comprehensive world maps of the medieval period, which depicted Africa, Asia, and Europe with remarkable accuracy for its time. The precision of Islamic cartography reflected both advanced mathematical knowledge and extensive trade networks that brought detailed information from distant regions. However, this knowledge was largely unavailable to Europeans during the medieval period, contributing to the geographic ignorance of late medieval Europe.

The Age of Exploration (15th-17th centuries) fundamentally transformed cartography. European explorers like Columbus, da Gama, and Magellan ventured into unknown oceans and brought back information that was urgently mapped and studied. Gerardus Mercator's projection, introduced in 1569, solved a critical technical problem: it represented the curved Earth on a flat surface in a way that preserved directional relationships, making it invaluable for navigation. However, Mercator's projection distorts the relative sizes of landmasses, particularly exaggerating the size of regions near the poles. This distortion has had lasting consequences, influencing European perceptions of global geography and, critics argue, reinforcing cultural assumptions about the relative importance of different regions.

The development of precise instruments and mathematical techniques in the 17th and 18th centuries — including the marine chronometer, the sextant, and refined trigonometry — allowed cartographers to determine longitude and latitude with unprecedented accuracy. This technological advancement transformed maps from artistic representations into scientifically rigorous documents. By the 19th century, national governments began systematic survey projects to map their territories exhaustively. The Ordnance Survey, established in Britain in 1791, created detailed large-scale maps that became templates for similar national mapping projects worldwide.

Twentieth and twenty-first century cartography has been revolutionised by satellite imagery, GPS technology, and digital mapping. Satellites provide unprecedented detail of Earth's surface and can track changes over time. GPS technology enables precise positioning anywhere on the globe. Digital mapping platforms allow users not merely to view static maps but to manipulate them, layer different types of information, and interact with spatial data. These technological advances have democratised map-making; anyone with basic digital tools can now create maps, whereas cartography was once the exclusive domain of skilled professionals and wealthy institutions. Yet the digital era has also raised new questions about data accuracy, privacy, and whose knowledge gets represented in digital maps.

passages.title: Epidemics and Pandemics in History
passages.text:
Epidemics and pandemics — disease outbreaks affecting large populations across broad geographic areas — have fundamentally shaped human history. More people have died from infectious disease than from all wars, famines, and natural disasters combined. Understanding the history of major epidemics reveals how disease interacts with human societies, how populations respond to crisis, and how scientific understanding of disease has evolved. Major historical epidemics have caused demographic catastrophes, triggered economic disruption, shifted political power, and accelerated social change.

The Black Death, a bubonic plague pandemic that swept through Europe, Asia, and Africa in the 14th century, was among the most devastating epidemics in recorded history. Spread by fleas living on rats, the plague killed an estimated 75 to 200 million people worldwide, including approximately 30 to 60 percent of Europe's population. The scale of death was so vast that it triggered profound social reorganisation: labour shortages increased wages for surviving workers, feudal hierarchies weakened as survivors could demand better conditions, and the cultural trauma was reflected in religious questioning and artistic expressions of mortality. The plague also demonstrated how global trade networks could rapidly spread disease; the same merchant ships that carried silk and spices also carried plague-infected rats.

The 16th-century introduction of smallpox to the Americas by European explorers had catastrophic consequences for indigenous populations. Native Americans had no previous exposure to smallpox and thus no immunity, making them extraordinarily susceptible. Combined with warfare and displacement caused by colonisation, smallpox and other introduced diseases killed an estimated 90 percent of the indigenous population in the Americas within a century of contact. This biological catastrophe fundamentally altered the hemisphere's demographics, economics, and political systems. The pandemic illustrates how disease vulnerability depends on prior exposure and population immunity — a principle that remained poorly understood until the 20th century.

The cholera pandemics of the 19th century killed millions but also advanced scientific understanding of disease transmission. In 1854, British physician John Snow conducted a landmark epidemiological investigation of a cholera outbreak in London. By mapping deaths and tracking the contamination of a particular water pump, Snow demonstrated that cholera was transmitted through contaminated water, not through "bad air" (miasma) as was widely believed. His work established modern epidemiological methods and provided evidence for germ theory, though his findings were initially resisted by the medical establishment. The institutional response to cholera — improving urban sanitation and water treatment infrastructure — demonstrated how scientific understanding could translate into public health improvements.

The 1918 influenza pandemic, also called the Spanish Flu, infected one-third of the global population and killed between 50 to 100 million people, far more than World War I was killing at the time. The pandemic spread rapidly along military supply lines and trade routes during World War I. Modern analysis using genetic sequencing of preserved virus samples has revealed that the 1918 flu virus, while unusually virulent, did not fundamentally differ from typical influenza viruses — its impact derived from its rapid spread through a densely interconnected global population. The pandemic illustrated the vulnerability of modern, densely populated societies to infectious disease and accelerated the professionalization of public health as a discipline.

The modern era has brought improved capacity to respond to epidemics through vaccines, antibiotics, and disease surveillance systems. The eradication of smallpox in 1980 — achieved through coordinated global vaccination campaigns — stands as one of humanity's greatest public health triumphs. However, emerging infectious diseases continue to pose threats. Tuberculosis remains one of the leading infectious disease killers, drug-resistant microorganisms are spreading, and zoonotic diseases — infections jumping from animals to humans — continue to emerge unpredictably. The COVID-19 pandemic, beginning in 2019, reminded the world that despite modern medicine and technology, large-scale disease outbreaks remain possible and have profound social, economic, and political consequences.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, what does the history of cartography reveal?
questions.correctAnswer: What knowledge societies valued and how they organised space
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states that cartography 'reveals not only where places are, but also what knowledge societies valued, how they organised space, and what they believed about distant regions.'
options: What knowledge societies valued and how they organised space
Nothing relevant to modern geography
Merely artistic representations without practical value
Only accurate location information

questions.prompt: The word 'illuminates' in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: 'Illuminates' metaphorically means to make clear or reveal understanding, as history of cartography illuminates broader questions.
options: literally shines light on
clarifies or sheds light on
obscures or hides
decorates with light

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, when did Eratosthenes calculate Earth's circumference?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states 'Eratosthenes calculated Earth's circumference with remarkable accuracy around 240 BCE.'
options: During the medieval period
Around 300 BCE
Around 240 BCE
Around 100 BCE

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about knowledge transmission during the medieval period?
questions.correctAnswer: Islamic geographical knowledge was not readily available to medieval Europeans
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 states Islamic cartography was achieved but 'this knowledge was largely unavailable to Europeans during the medieval period, contributing to the geographic ignorance of late medieval Europe.'
options: Europeans had superior geographical knowledge to Arabs
Knowledge sharing was universal in the medieval period
All medieval societies shared geographical knowledge equally
Islamic geographical knowledge was not readily available to medieval Europeans

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention Mercator's projection in paragraph 4?
questions.correctAnswer: To illustrate a technological solution to a mapping problem and its consequences
questions.explanation: Mercator's projection is discussed as solving navigation challenges but also creating geographic distortions with lasting cultural effects.
options: To illustrate a technological solution to a mapping problem and its consequences
To show that modern maps are identical to those from the 16th century
To explain why exploration was impossible
To argue that all map projections are equally accurate

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 4, what is NOT mentioned as an effect of Mercator's projection?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 states the projection was 'invaluable for navigation' and created distortions, but does not say it made navigation impossible.
options: It distorted the relative sizes of landmasses
It made navigation impossible
It exaggerated polar regions
It preserved directional relationships

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, what were the primary purposes of early Babylonian maps?
questions.correctAnswer: To track land holdings and support agricultural irrigation
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states Babylonian maps 'primarily represent[ed] property and natural features relevant to agricultural irrigation.'
options: To record religious teachings
For artistic decoration only
To track land holdings and support agricultural irrigation
For military conquest only

questions.prompt: The word 'synthesised' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: 'Synthesised' means to combine various elements into a unified whole, as Strabo combined geographic knowledge.
options: separated into parts
criticized harshly
created from nothing
combined or integrated

questions.prompt: Which best expresses the essential information in this sentence: 'The Islamic Golden Age, spanning from roughly the 8th to 14th centuries, was a period of extraordinary cartographic achievement.'
questions.correctAnswer: Between the 8th and 14th centuries, Islamic societies made remarkable advances in map-making
questions.explanation: The sentence indicates exceptional cartographic progress during a defined historical period in Islamic civilisation.
options: Between the 8th and 14th centuries, Islamic societies made remarkable advances in map-making
Islamic societies had no interest in cartography
Modern cartography is inferior to the Islamic period
Map-making was invented during the Islamic Golden Age

questions.prompt: Complete a summary of the passage. Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas.
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes cartography's cultural significance (A), technological evolution (C), and how maps reflect knowledge systems (E).
options: A. Cartography reveals societal knowledge systems and how different cultures organised space.
B. Ancient maps were entirely inaccurate and have no historical value.
C. Technological innovations like Mercator's projection and satellite imagery transformed mapping capabilities.
D. Map-making has remained unchanged throughout human history.
E. From ancient times through the digital era, cartography has reflected advances in mathematics, exploration, and technology.
F. Only Islamic cartographers ever made accurate maps.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, what is a key difference between epidemics and pandemics?
questions.correctAnswer: Pandemics affect large populations across broad geographic areas
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 defines pandemics as 'disease outbreaks affecting large populations across broad geographic areas,' distinguishing them from localised epidemics.
options: Epidemics are more deadly than pandemics
Pandemics affect large populations across broad geographic areas
There is no difference between the two terms
Epidemics only occur in modern times

questions.prompt: The word 'triggered' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: 'Triggered' means to cause or initiate, as the Black Death triggered social reorganisation.
options: gradually eliminated
delayed indefinitely
caused or set in motion
completely prevented

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, how was the Black Death spread?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states 'Spread by fleas living on rats, the plague killed an estimated 75 to 200 million people worldwide.'
options: Through direct human contact only
Via infected insects in grain stores
Through contaminated water supplies
By fleas living on rats

questions.prompt: Why does the author discuss John Snow in paragraph 4?
questions.correctAnswer: To illustrate how epidemiological investigation advanced scientific understanding of disease transmission
questions.explanation: Snow's cholera investigation is presented as establishing modern epidemiological methods and demonstrating waterborne transmission.
options: To illustrate how epidemiological investigation advanced scientific understanding of disease transmission
To argue that public health interventions are never effective
To explain why modern medicine is powerless against disease
To show that cholera was the deadliest disease in history

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about indigenous American populations at the time of European contact?
questions.correctAnswer: They lacked immunity to European diseases due to lack of prior exposure
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 states 'Native Americans had no previous exposure to smallpox and thus no immunity, making them extraordinarily susceptible.'
options: They had been exposed to smallpox previously
They lacked immunity to European diseases due to lack of prior exposure
Disease immunity is not genetically determined
They had superior immune systems to Europeans

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 5, when did the eradication of smallpox occur?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 states 'The eradication of smallpox in 1980 — achieved through coordinated global vaccination campaigns.'

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, which is NOT mentioned as a consequence of the Black Death in Europe?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 mentions labour shortages, wage increases, feudal weakening, and cultural trauma, but not increased agricultural production.
options: Labour shortages and increased wages
Weakening of feudal hierarchies
Cultural trauma and religious questioning
Increased agricultural production

questions.prompt: The word 'catastrophe' in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: 'Catastrophe' refers to a sudden, disastrous event causing great damage, like smallpox decimating indigenous populations.
options: a sudden disaster
a planned strategy
a religious festival
a natural achievement

questions.prompt: Which best expresses the essential information in this sentence: 'By mapping deaths and tracking the contamination of a particular water pump, Snow demonstrated that cholera was transmitted through contaminated water, not through "bad air" (miasma) as was widely believed.'
questions.correctAnswer: Snow used mapping techniques to show cholera spreads through water, contrary to prevailing belief
questions.explanation: The sentence describes Snow's method and his key finding that contradicted contemporary medical theory.
options: Snow invented the concept of cholera
Snow used mapping techniques to show cholera spreads through water, contrary to prevailing belief
The miasma theory of disease was always correct
Water contamination plays no role in cholera transmission

questions.prompt: Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas in the passage.
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes disease as a major historical force (A), that epidemics have triggered social change (C), and that scientific understanding improves response (D).
options: A. Major epidemics throughout history have killed millions and profoundly affected societies.
B. The Black Death and smallpox were the only significant epidemics in human history.
C. Epidemics trigger demographic, economic, and political consequences that reshape societies.
D. Scientific advances in understanding disease transmission enable better public health responses.
E. Modern medicine has completely eliminated all infectious disease threats.
F. Indigenous populations in the Americas were naturally immune to all European diseases.
